This article compares the types of re-operations performed on patients with Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD), serving as indicator 6 in the Danish IBD registry. The data provides a cross-sectional breakdown of specific surgical procedure codes, detailing both the absolute number of procedures (Antal) and their relative frequency (Procent) among all recorded re-operations [^src1].

The most common re-operation is [[kjah01-laparoskopi|KJAH01]] (Laparoscopy), which leads the dataset with 21 procedures, accounting for 27.3% of the total [^src1]. This is closely followed by [[kjah00-eksplorativ-laparotomi|KJAH00]] (Explorative laparotomy) with 18 procedures, representing 23.4% [^src1]. Together, these two major surgical approaches constitute over half of all re-operations performed on this patient cohort, acting as a clear outlier pattern where a small fraction of procedure codes dominates the clinical reality [^src1].

Following the leaders, the frequency of specific re-operations drops significantly. [[kjff13-terminal-enterostomi]] (Terminal enterostomy) ranks third with 6 procedures (7.8%), while [[kjwa00-sutur-af-saarruptur-eft-gastroenterologisk-operatio]] (Suture of wound rupture after gastroenterological operation) accounts for 4 procedures (5.2%) [^src1]. [[kjfa70-sutur-af-tyndtarm]] (Suture of small intestine) and [[kjww96-anden-reoperation-eft-gastroenterologisk-operation]] (Other reoperation after gastroenterological operation) each record 3 procedures, making up 3.9% respectively [^src1].

The remaining 16 procedure types listed in the registry act as trailers in this comparison; their individual counts and percentages are suppressed or marked with a hash (`#`), indicating that the number of occurrences was too low to be reported individually or was zero [^src1]. Because this comparison is drawn from a single reporting period in the 2025 DANIBD registry, it is not possible to identify longitudinal trends, improvements, or declines in re-operation types over time [^src1]. Furthermore, the registry data strictly provides a snapshot of surgical reinterventions without establishing any specific performance targets, thresholds, or met/missed standards for these procedures [^src1].
